meta.title: Who really said "Cowards die many times before their deaths; the valiant never taste of death but once"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Shakespeare: Caesar speaks the line in Julius Caesar, Act 2 scene 2, first printed in the 1623 First Folio. The popular thousand-times wording is not his.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Cowards die many times before their deaths; the valiant never taste of death but once'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Shakespeare, usually misquoted. Caesar says it in Julius Caesar 2.2; the 1623 First Folio reads: Cowards dye many times before their deaths.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Caesar speaks the line to Calphurnia in Act 2, scene 2 of Julius Caesar, brushing off her dream and the night’s omens. It is in the play’s only early text, the 1623 First Folio ↗, at through-line numbers 1020–1021 — so the attribution and the wording both check out, which is unusual for a quote this famous.

source.heading: The source text

docMeta.dd: Act 2, scene 2 — Caesar answering Calphurnia (First Folio TLN 1020–1021)
First Folio, London, 1623 — no earlier quarto exists

source.excerpt:
CALPURNIA: When beggars die, there are no comets seen; / The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes.

CAESAR: Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once. / Of all the wonders that I yet have heard, / It seems to me most strange that men should fear, / Seeing that death, a necessary end, / Will come when it will come.
trail: The 1623 First Folio prints the lines in old spelling — “Cowards dye many times before their deaths, / The valiant neuer taste of death but once” — at through-line numbers 1020–1021 in the Internet Shakespeare Editions old-spelling transcription ↗, edited by John D. Cox.

There is nothing earlier to check against: the ISE textual introduction ↗ states that “Julius Caesar appeared in only one early version, and all subsequent texts are based on it. This is the version in the First Folio, printed in 1623.”

The Folger Shakespeare Library ↗ lists the line among its famous quotes from the play, gives the speaker as Caesar in Act 2, scene 2, and notes that Shakespeare “may have written Julius Caesar as the first of his plays to be performed at the Globe, in 1599.”
Independently, Project Gutenberg’s First Folio-derived text ↗ (eBook #1120) carries the same two lines in the same exchange with Calphurnia, in the same original spelling.
source.excerptNote: Modern-spelling text as given in the MIT Complete Works ↗. The 1623 Folio reads “Cowards dye many times before their deaths, / The valiant neuer taste of death but once”. Line numbering differs between modern editions, which is why the Folio’s through-line numbers are cited instead.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: Shakespeare wrote roughly three dozen plays for the London stage, most of them for the company that occupied the Globe from 1599. Julius Caesar is thought to have been written that year and may have been the first of his plays performed there. Eighteen of his plays, this one included, were never printed in his lifetime and survive only because two of his fellow actors gathered them into the First Folio of 1623 — which is the single reason this line exists to be quoted at all.

misattribution.heading: The attribution is right. The wording usually isn’t.
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous quotes where Shakespeare really is the author — so the errors have migrated from who to what. Three versions circulate that the Folio does not support.

items.who: “A coward dies a thousand times before his death”
items.why: This is the form most often shared, and it is credited squarely to Shakespeare: Goodreads carries it with 496 likes ↗, sourced to “William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar”, and even splices it onto Caesar’s later lines. No “thousand” and no “his death” appear in the Folio text, which reads “many times before their deaths”.

“The coward dies a thousand deaths, the brave but one” is widely filed under Hemingway — Goodreads credits it to him from A Farewell to Arms ↗. In the novel it is Frederic Henry reciting the tag as a question in chapter XXI ↗; when Catherine asks who said it, he answers “I don’t know.” Hemingway’s own line is Catherine’s rebuttal about the brave dying two thousand deaths.

The sentiment is routinely quoted as Shakespeare’s advice. In the play it is given to Caesar in Act 2, scene 2 ↗ to dismiss his wife’s warning — and he is assassinated in the following act. The dramatic point is that the speaker is wrong about his own safety, not that the maxim is endorsed.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine line, in the play’s only early printing, is “Cowards dye many times before their deaths, / The valiant neuer taste of death but once” — First Folio, 1623, TLN 1020–1021 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Caesar is being talked out of going to the Senate. Calphurnia has dreamed of his death, the augurers have found no heart in the sacrificed beast, and she has just told him that the heavens do not blaze for beggars. His reply is the most quotable thing he says in the play — and, structurally, the setup for the knives. Shakespeare gives his most confident line about death to the man who has one scene left to live.

That double edge is why the passage travelled beyond the theatre. When the political prisoner Sonny Venkatrathnam smuggled a Complete Works onto Robben Island as his one permitted book and passed it around the cells, inmates initialled their favourite passages. Nelson Mandela chose this one: the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust ↗ records that he marked it “M, December 16th 1977”.
detailsBody: Shakespeare built the speech out of Plutarch, whom he read in Sir Thomas North’s 1579 English translation. The ISE general introduction ↗ suggests the passage “may have been inspired” by Plutarch’s brief note that the day before he died Caesar, asked what death was best, “cried out aloud, ‘Death unlooked for’”.

The American Repertory Theater’s survey of the two texts sets the seed beside the harvest: North’s Caesar says “It was better to die once, than always to be afraid of death” ↗, and notes more generally that the language of Julius Caesar “owes a good deal to North, whom Shakespeare copied, paraphrased and versified.”
